about: Claims of the Thinking length investigation (TL-*) and of the CuteAFD v5 context probe (CP-*), generated from the results by tools/build_findings.py. Each evidence entry names a repository file and an RFC 6901 JSON pointer; 'value' is what the pointer resolved to at build time. tools/verify.py re-resolves every pointer and recomputes entries that carry 'recompute' from the per-reply tables.

status_vocabulary.measurement: frozen rule: protocol and decision rule frozen (hashes in the run's protocol/FROZEN.json) before the first request
status_vocabulary.measurement: post hoc: computed from frozen-run data after the run; not part of any decision rule
status_vocabulary.measurement: descriptive: counted from frozen-run data; not part of any decision rule
status_vocabulary.exploratory: run kind exploratory: useful evidence, not a frozen comparison
status_vocabulary.source reading: read in source code and logs, no measurement
status_vocabulary.judgement: source and measurements: a conclusion drawn from source reading and published measurements together; not isolated by a run of its own

conventions.interval: 95% bootstrap over the unit in ci_over (percentile); 4,000 draws for TL-* entries, 10,000 for CP-* entries; TL-* seeds are in each run's protocol; CP-* entries use seed 5 with percentile indices 250 and 9749 (frozen rule), and seed 7 or 20261111 with indices 250 and 9750 (post hoc and by-family readings), stated per entry in recompute.bootstrap and in analysis/posthoc.py
conventions.detected: interval excludes the null (1 for ratios, 0 for differences)
conventions.pointers: RFC 6901: split on '/', then replace '~1' with '/' and '~0' with '~' (keys such as 'C-K6x/V-BF16' contain a slash)

definitions.finished: finish_reason == 'stop' and hit_cap == False (a reply that ended on its own under the 130,048-token cap)
definitions.reasoning_tokens: tokens of the reasoning text, by re-tokenizing it with the model's tokenizer
definitions.seed_paired_ratio: for each (prompt, rep) where both arms finished: log(reasoning tokens A / B); ratio = exp(mean over all such pairs); interval: bootstrap over prompts (resample prompts with replacement, pool their pairs)
definitions.bootstrap_draws: rng = random.Random(seed); each draw: rng.choice(sorted prompt list) repeated once per prompt, mean of the pooled log ratios; sort the 4,000 draw means; interval = exp of values at indices 100 and 3899
definitions.cross_engine_ratio: post hoc: for each (prompt, rep) where both finished: log(A / B); mean within each prompt; mean over prompts; exp. Each prompt weighs the same, so a same-engine contrast differs slightly from seed_paired_ratio
definitions.pass_pairs: post hoc: for each (prompt, rep) where both arms finished: all_tests_pass A minus B (1, 0 or -1); mean over the pairs; interval: bootstrap over prompts as bootstrap_draws, on the pooled differences (seed 20261108)
definitions.engine_comparison: vLLM ratio / CuteAFD ratio = exp(mean over prompts of [vLLM prompt log ratio - CuteAFD prompt log ratio])

context_probe.applies_to: CP-* entries (results/2026-11-10-context-probe); the definitions above apply to TL-* entries
context_probe.rows_used: analysis/samples.csv rows with final == 1 and status == ok (one per request; delivery turns of the eight-turn pass have final == 0); for the reference checkpoint, the same rows of analysis/samples-reference.csv beside them
context_probe.request_score: correct / fields if finish_class == 'stop' and fields > 0, else 0 (a reply that hit the cap or was ended by the loop abort scores 0)
context_probe.item_paired_difference_frozen: for each item, over the (pass, length) cells in recompute.passes x recompute.lengths where both arms have a row: request_score(b) - request_score(a); mean within the item (statistics.fmean); estimate = mean over items, rounded to 4 places. Interval: items in sorted order, rng = random.Random(5); 10,000 draws, each the fmean of n values vals[rng.randrange(n)]; sorted draws at indices 250 and 9749
context_probe.item_paired_difference_pooled: post hoc: items of recompute.family (all items if absent), sorted; per item and arm, the mean over passes x lengths of request_score (or of every_field_right when strict); d = b - a per item; estimate = sum(d) / n. Interval: rng = random.Random(seed); 10,000 draws, each sum of n values d[rng.randrange(n)] / n; sorted draws at indices 250 and 9750
context_probe.sign: 'b - a': above 0 = arm b scored higher

passes.turns-p8-rep0: the same records delivered over eight turns, then the question

findings.question: What differs between CuteAFD's two core formats besides the core's weights?
findings.answer: With a BF16 core, CuteAFD v4.0.0's launcher also puts the KDA projections (including three gate projections outside the core) and the vocabulary head in FP8, and prefill runs the MLA and MLP projections with FP8 activations; with the native 6-bit core these stay on the 6-bit kernels or in BF16. On a two-GPU head split the FP8 KDA path also comes with KDA output sharding, which v4 accepts only with FP8 KDA and clears for the native core. These are the launcher's defaults (its comment at run-family.sh:2337-2351, v4.0.0), with the author's stated reasons: decode speed and pool size, and output sharding to avoid rounding the GPUs' partial outputs, checked on teacher-forced top-1 and KL. The model notes (docs/models/glm5_flash.md 'Default precision') and the --kda-fp8 option text (mod.rs:189-197) describe BF16 KDA as the two-GPU default; the documents differ, and the launcher's choice is what runs.

evidence.what: source and launch-log reading with file:line references

findings.question: Which part of CuteAFD's FP8 path goes with the shorter code reasoning of the BF16-core checkpoint (local derived checkpoint, not a producer release)?
findings.answer: The KDA launch setting: switching the KDA projections from FP8 to BF16 (on this two-GPU layout that also turns off KDA output sharding, which v4 runs only with FP8 KDA) gives 1.31x [1.24, 1.38], detected, every prompt above 1; then the vocabulary head 1.02x [0.97, 1.07] and prefill activations 0.99x [0.97, 1.02], not detected. With the KDA setting off the gap to the native 6-bit core closes (C-K6 / F-kda 0.96x [0.92, 1.01]); KDA's share of the gap 1.16 [0.95, 1.37] (above 1 = the point estimate passes the native core; the interval includes 1, consistent with the whole gap). Settings were switched off cumulatively.

findings.question: Across the code-thinking arms of both engines, does passing all hidden tests differ in paired replies?
findings.answer: Post hoc, every contrast looked at (13): the arms with CuteAFD's FP8 settings switched off (F-kda, F-head, F-pre) and the vLLM BF16 core pass more often than both CuteAFD code-study arms; 5 of 13 intervals exclude 0, all that way, and 2 after allowing for 13 looks (F-pre, all three settings off, against each code-study arm). The two CuteAFD cores, a fifth apart in reasoning length, pass equally often: passing does not follow length, and the native core (none of the FP8 settings) passes about as often as the FP8-from-BF16 core.

findings.question: Where in CuteAFD does the code-length difference arise: prefill or generation?
findings.answer: Most likely on the generation path (decode and speculative verify); prefill is not excluded. Prompts are 1,155-1,758 tokens against medians of 50-68K reasoning tokens; speculative verify steps run on the decode programs, which read the FP8 KDA copies, and KDA output sharding is not limited to prefill. The KDA setting also changes the KDA projections in prefill, and the prompt's recurrent state seeds every later token. Not separated: KDA in prefill against generation, plain decode against speculative verify.

findings.question: Does accuracy fall with context length, and does core precision produce the fall?
findings.answer: It falls in every arm, the BF16 reference included: field score 0.98 at 4K and 0.89 to 0.91 at 127K. The reference loses about as much as the other arms (0.08 against 0.07 and 0.09), so core precision does not produce it. A third to a half of the loss is replies that did not finish (cap or repetition abort, scored 0): among finished replies the 127K score is anchor 0.942, hqa 0.936, compact 0.928. Where the rest sits is open: the arms share the model, the K4 experts, the engine, the drafter, the sampling settings and the reply cap.

findings.question: Did the eight-turn pass test a conversation whose history the model wrote?
findings.answer: No. Decode ran in every reply, but the model's own turns were a median 9% of the final prompt at 4K and 0.3-0.4% at 127K: at long context over 99% of the history was written by prefill. What the pass shows is split delivery: delivering the same input as eight messages shows no accuracy cost (16K to 127K: every interval includes 0, a cost up to about 0.07 is not excluded; 4K: eight turns score slightly higher in anchor and hqa, intervals exclude 0). The turn design is to be revised.

result.name: model-written share of the final prompt, median over 60 sessions

evidence.value: Decode ran in every reply of every pass. What the 8-turn pass did not exercise is history written by decode: the model's own turns (thinking included, which stays in context) are a median 9% of the final prompt at 4K, 2.7% at 16K, 0.7% at 64K and 0.3-0.4% at 127K, so at long context more than 99% of the history the final answer was conditioned on was written by prefill. The pass measures split delivery of the same input. It does not test a conversation whose history the model wrote (protocol question 3). The turn design is to be revised.
design to be revised; the protocol's advance reading ("turn check v2 not needed") is withdrawn

findings.question: How does a native EXLR8 K4 checkpoint of the same model, served by the same engine, score on the same graded tasks from 4K to 127K tokens?
findings.answer: No difference measured from anchor or hqa: +0.006 [-0.007, +0.019] against anchor and +0.006 [-0.008, +0.019] against hqa. Against compact its field score is higher post hoc: +0.016 [+0.004, +0.029] over four lengths, +0.030 [+0.006, +0.056] at 64K and 127K pooled, +0.002 [-0.006, +0.009] at 4K and 16K. That is a lead, not a finding: the checkpoint was added after the results were read, and this is one of 84 intervals computed without correction, of which 3 exclude 0 (all exlr8-k4 - compact on field score). It is on the partial-credit score only: on every field right the pair does not separate (+0.025 [-0.017, +0.065]). exlr8-k4 is a different checkpoint from the three probe arms, not a setting of the same one. Any difference from a probe arm is a whole-checkpoint difference and is not attributable to one component. Basis: two single-message passes, 60 items, 480 requests per arm, 0 errors, prompt tokens equal to anchor's on every request; strength: low for the difference from compact (post hoc, one of many intervals), moderate for the absence of a measured difference from anchor and hqa (one model family, synthetic tasks, intervals of about 0.013 either side).

findings.question: With the engine scoring given texts instead of generating, does the EXLR8 K4 reference checkpoint predict the text worse than the three probe arms, and how far apart are the arms?
findings.answer: Not measurably worse at predicting the text: over the whole capture the most likely token is the given one as often as for anchor (-0.0007 [-0.0037, +0.0023] on the prefill path; the interval spans 0 on both paths); values by depth band are published without intervals. Its mean NLL is lower than anchor's (-0.0134 [-0.0199, -0.0070] nats, prefill path), which is not read as an improvement: 99 of 9,728 positions carry -91.48 of the -130.40 nat (70% of the sum), the median per-position difference is 0 and the arm is ahead on fewer than half of the positions. Distance from the unquantized BF16 model is not measured for these four configurations in this run; the repository's BF16-referenced panels (texts to 14.4K tokens) cover other checkpoints. Between arms, which is not a distance from the BF16 model: the three probe arms share their experts, so the distance between two of them reflects the settings outside the experts alone, the core and for anchor the output head (prefill path, median KL 0.0004 to 0.0006, most likely token different on 4.20% to 5.15% of positions); exlr8-k4 has its own experts, so its distance to any probe arm (0.0015 to 0.0017; 8.83% to 8.88%) includes both expert quantizations and does not rank it against the probe arms by closeness to the BF16 model. exlr8-k4 is a different checkpoint from the three probe arms, not a setting of the same one. Any difference from a probe arm is a whole-checkpoint difference and is not attributable to one component. Basis: one capture per arm, five texts (not the task items), assistant frame; strength: low (exploratory, one capture, no correction for the number of comparisons).
